issues.legal_issue: A transaction in which a husband provides the purchase money for property registered in his wife's name is not benami unless the evidence, assessed as a whole, establishes that he intended the wife to hold title only nominally.
material_facts: The property was conveyed in the wife's name, and the Court assessed the case on the assumption that the husband provided the purchase money.
The wife’s power of attorney stated that she had decided to purchase the property; her husband witnessed it and she was described as her father’s daughter rather than as his wife.
The wife was recorded as owner, possessed the property, paid taxes and participated in its construction; the husband had no evident need to conceal assets or avoid liability.

The husband made his wife the nominee under his life insurance policy, and the children later sought mutation in their names as heirs; the son objected but did not pursue the matter after mutation was allowed.
One daughter gave evidence supporting the mother’s ownership; the son’s wife did not testify, and the only other defence witness was born long after the purchase and lacked personal knowledge of it.
issues.conclusion: The evidence showed that the husband intended the property to benefit his wife, not that she was a benamidar. The burden of proving a benami transaction rested on those alleging it, and they did not discharge it. The judgment reversing the trial court was set aside and the trial court’s decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The person alleging a benami transaction bears the serious burden of proving it; the person named as purchaser begins with the presumption that the apparent state of affairs is real. Intention is central and must be inferred from the totality of the evidence, including the source of purchase money, possession and nature of the property, motive, parties’ relationship, custody of title deeds and subsequent conduct. The source of funds is important but is not conclusive by itself. The Court relied on Jaydayal Poddar v. Mst. Bibi Hazira, (1974) 1 SCC 3; Thakur Bhim Singh v. Thakur Kan Singh, (1980) 3 SCC 72; Valliammal v. Subramaniam, (2004) 7 SCC 233; Kanakarathanammal v. V.S. Loganatha Mudaliar, AIR 1965 SC 271; and Tulsi v. Chandrika Prasad, (2006) 8 SCC 322, including its principle on drawing an adverse inference where a party who could give material evidence does not testify.

rule.if: benami_title_dispute and purchaser_named_as_owner and (owner_exercised_ownership or transaction_documents_support_owner_intent) and no_compelling_evidence_of_nominal_ownership

predicates.benami_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns an allegation that a person named as purchaser holds property only for another person.
predicates.purchaser_named_as_owner: The conveyance identifies the person whose ownership is disputed as the purchaser or owner.
predicates.owner_exercised_ownership: The named owner possessed, managed, or dealt with the property as an owner after purchase.
predicates.transaction_documents_support_owner_inte: Documents or circumstances connected with the purchase indicate that the named owner was intended to benefit from it.
predicates.no_compelling_evidence_of_nominal_owners: The party alleging nominal ownership did not produce compelling evidence that the named owner was intended to hold title only for another.

issues.definition: When a named purchaser exercises ownership or the transaction supports the intention that the purchaser benefit, and there is no compelling evidence of nominal ownership, the named purchaser is treated as the beneficial owner.

issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer who relies on ouster or adverse possession must prove possession hostile to the other co-sharers’ title; failure to do so does not defeat their title.
material_facts: The son asserted that the property belonged to him and pleaded ouster, while the daughters claimed shares as heirs of their mother.
The son objected when the daughters’ names were entered in the municipal records, but the mutation was allowed and he took no further step to challenge it.
The record did not establish possession that clearly denied the other co-sharers’ title.
issues.conclusion: The plea of ouster was not established, and the son could not thereby defeat the other co-sharers’ title.
issues.legal_principle: Adverse possession requires hostile possession that denies the true owner’s title; the person asserting it must prove that hostility by clear and unequivocal evidence. A claimant who is uncertain of the true owner cannot establish hostile possession against that owner. The Court relied on T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, (2006) 7 SCC 570, as well as Govindammal v. R. Perumal Chettiar, (2006) 11 SCC 600; P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma, decided 24 April 2007; and Syed Abdul Khader v. Rami Reddy, (1979) 2 SCC 601.

predicates.co_sharer_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to property among persons asserting co-sharer interests.
predicates.ouster_or_adverse_possession_claimed: One co-sharer claims to have excluded the others or to have acquired title through adverse possession.
predicates.clear_hostile_denial_of_other_sharers_ti: The claimant clearly and unequivocally possessed the property in denial of the other co-sharers’ title.

issues.definition: If a co-sharer claims ouster or adverse possession but has not clearly and unequivocally denied the other co-sharers’ title through hostile possession, their title is not defeated.

issues.legal_issue: The rule that an immovable-property gift may not become a wife’s stridhan under Dayabhaga law does not prohibit a husband from gifting money for a purchase in her name and does not establish that the purchase was benami.
material_facts: The property was purchased in the wife’s name, and the Court proceeded on the assumption that the husband provided the purchase money.
The High Court relied on Dayabhaga law to reason that the husband could not have gifted the property to his wife.
The Court distinguished a gift of purchase money from a gift of the immovable property itself and held the asserted limitation on stridhan irrelevant to whether the transaction was benami.
issues.conclusion: The Dayabhaga-based reasoning did not support the finding that the transaction was benami; a husband could gift the money used to purchase property for his wife, and that issue did not determine the nature of the transaction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that Dayabhaga law’s treatment of an immovable-property gift as not becoming the wife’s stridhan concerns inheritance and succession, not whether a transaction is benami; the money used to buy property may be gifted to the wife. It relied on Kanakarathanammal v. V.S. Loganatha Mudaliar, AIR 1965 SC 271, and K.K. Das, Receiver v. Sm. Amina Khatun Bibi, AIR 1940 Cal 356, and noted the Transfer of Property Act’s treatment of restrictions on transfer.

rule.if: benami_title_dispute and property_purchased_in_wifes_name and husband_provided_purchase_money and dayabhaga_stridhan_rule_invoked

predicates.benami_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether property registered in one person’s name is held benami for another.
predicates.property_purchased_in_wifes_name: The property was purchased and registered in the wife’s name.
predicates.husband_provided_purchase_money: The husband supplied the money used to purchase the property.
predicates.dayabhaga_stridhan_rule_invoked: A party relies on the rule that an immovable-property gift does not become the wife’s stridhan under Dayabhaga law.

issues.definition: When property is purchased in a wife’s name with money provided by her husband, reliance on the Dayabhaga rule about stridhan does not establish that the transaction was benami.
